Name: premature_lexicalization
Title: Right Concept, Wrong Word: Premature Lexical Commitment as a Distinct Knowledge-Retrieval Failure in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When answering factual queries, LLMs internally select the correct target entity as an abstract, token-agnostic concept representation, but the final answer is produced through a separate, later lexicalization step that maps concept to first output token. We hypothesize a distinct failure mode—premature lexicalization—in which the model commits to a high-prior or low-perplexity first token before the concept representation is fully resolved, causing it to emit a lexically-adjacent wrong entity (one sharing the committed first token/subword) even though the correct concept was internally selected. We predict (1) the concept selection and lexical commitment are dissociable and decodable at different layers, (2) a substantial fraction of factual errors are 'right-concept-wrong-word' cases where the correct entity is decodable as a concept but is out-competed at the lexicalization stage by a first-token-sharing distractor, and (3) delaying/re-weighting the lexical commitment (suppressing the prematurely-committed first token direction) recovers the correct entity more selectively than weight editing.
Related Work: A large body of work studies layer-wise commitment: 'Guess-then-Refine' (2025) shows early layers propose high-frequency tokens later refined; Iterative Inference / commitment-depth studies (2024–2026) track when models lock in answers; 'How LLMs Use Their Depth' (2025) shows first tokens of multi-token facts need more depth. Geva et al. (2023) describe attribute extraction via attention over an enriched subject. Concept-vs-language separation has been studied for multilingual models (language-agnostic concept spaces) but not for the concept-vs-lexeme distinction within a single language for factual recall. Confidence Regulation / entropy neurons (2024) and token-frequency effects on recall are documented. None of these identify premature lexicalization—a specific dissociation between token-agnostic concept selection and first-token lexical commitment—as a concrete, predictable factual-error mode, nor propose suppressing a prematurely-committed first-token direction as a non-destructive fix. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (expression gating, format-bound copies, candidate competition among entities, route arbitration, pre-retrieval familiarity, property collapse): here the failure is not choosing the wrong entity but choosing the wrong *word* for a correctly-chosen entity, driven by first-token statistics.
Abstract: Large language models sometimes produce a factual answer that is close to but not the correct entity—e.g., a name that shares a first syllable or subword with the right one. We propose that some of these errors reflect a distinct, overlooked mechanism: premature lexicalization. Under this view, factual recall proceeds in two stages—selecting the target entity as a token-agnostic concept, then lexicalizing that concept into output tokens—and errors arise when the model commits to a high-prior first token before the concept is fully resolved, emitting a lexically-adjacent wrong entity while the correct concept was internally selected. We test three claims. (1) Dissociability: a concept probe (predicting the correct entity in a token-agnostic representation, e.g., via aliases/paraphrastic descriptions) and a lexical probe (predicting the committed first output token) are separable and become decodable at different layers, with concept selection preceding or coexisting with a later lexical-commitment surge. (2) Prevalence: 'right-concept-wrong-word' errors—where the correct entity is decodable as a concept yet the output is a first-token-sharing distractor—form an identifiable fraction of factual errors, concentrated where the correct entity's first token is high-perplexity/rare and a distractor shares a common first token, above frequency-matched baselines. (3) Intervention: suppressing the prematurely-committed distractor first-token direction (or re-scoring the first token conditioned on the concept representation) recovers correct entities with higher specificity and less collateral damage than ROME editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions, evaluating probe separability, layer-onset ordering, error-type prevalence, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - concept and lexical signals are decodable at different layers): Tests that a token-agnostic concept representation becomes decodable before the first-token lexical commitment. Data: PopQA (14,282), T-REx/LAMA (~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); sample 9,000 facts whose answer entity has >=2 attested aliases/paraphrastic descriptions, fewer than the pool because alias sets are needed for the concept probe. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; two trainable per-layer probes on the last-token residual - a concept probe (target: a shared concept ID invariant across aliases, trained on one surface form and tested on held-out aliases) and a lexical probe (target: the emitted first token); seeds 0/1/2, label-shuffle and alias-shuffle controls. Systems compared: concept vs. lexical onset layers, bootstrap CIs. Decisive metric: onset-layer difference (first-layer at AUROC>=0.7) between concept and the lexical-commitment surge (first, concept should precede); supporting: per-layer accuracy/AUROC. Convincing: concept onset precedes lexical commitment by >=3 layers with non-overlapping CIs, both above shuffle. Undecidable band: a 1-3 layer gap or overlapping CIs cannot separate timing from probe difficulty - defer precedence to the causal test (Experiment 4). Negative: lexical onset at/before concept, or concept at alias-shuffle level, falsifies H1.

Experiment 2 (H1 - concept and lexical directions carry non-redundant information): Tests they are not collinear. Data: the residual activations from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; cross-linear-predictability and residualization of the two directions, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: concept predicting the correct entity before vs. after removing first-token-predictive variance. Decisive metric: retained concept->entity accuracy after residualizing out lexical variance (first); supporting: direction cosine similarity. Convincing: concept still predicts the correct entity at >=0.7 relative accuracy after residualization and cosine <=0.5. Undecidable band: retained accuracy 0.5-0.7 or cosine 0.5-0.75 indicates partial entanglement - report graded separability. Negative: retained accuracy <=0.5 or cosine >0.75 means the two collapse to one signal, falsifying the two-stage claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 - right-concept-wrong-word errors are a substantial, statistically distinct share): Tests that many errors are concept-correct but lexically out-competed by a first-token-sharing distractor. Data: model errors on Experiment 1 facts. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify errors into (a) premature-lexicalization (concept probe recovers the correct entity but the emitted answer shares the early committed first token/subword with a distractor), (b) genuine wrong-concept, (c) other. Systems compared: type-(a) rate when the correct entity's first token is rare and a competitor shares a common first token, against a null controlling for entity frequency and overall lexical similarity (logistic regression / chi-square). Decisive metric: fraction of errors that are premature-lexicalization, above the matched null (first); supporting: odds ratio with the rare-correct-token / shared-distractor-token condition. Convincing: >=20% of errors are premature-lexicalization, >=10 points above the null, with the predicted first-token-statistics dependence. Undecidable band: 8-20% above a null gap <10 points means the mode is real but minor - narrow H2 to a secondary mode. Negative: <8% or null-indistinguishable means the failure is not distinct from wrong-concept errors, falsifying H2.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 - the failure lives in lexicalization, not concept selection): Causally dissociates the two stages. Data: premature-lexicalization failures (target 1,200) plus wrong-concept failures (target 1,200) from Experiment 3. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; (a) patch the concept representation from a correct run into a premature-lexicalization failure (should NOT fix it if the failure is lexical), (b) suppress the distractor's first-token direction at the commitment layers (should fix it), (c) amplify the concept direction alone; random-direction control. Systems compared: concept-patch vs. first-token-suppression vs. concept-amplification vs. random, on the two failure types. Decisive metric: fix-rate gap = first-token-suppression fix rate minus concept-patch fix rate on premature-lexicalization failures (first, the causal signature); supporting: the reverse pattern on wrong-concept failures. Convincing: on premature-lexicalization failures, first-token suppression fixes >=35% while concept patching fixes <=10% (gap >=25 points), and the pattern reverses for wrong-concept failures. Undecidable band: a 10-25 point gap means partial localization - report weak causal support. Negative: no gap, or concept patching fixing as much as suppression, means the failure is not lexicalization-stage, falsifying the H1/H2 mechanism.

Experiment 5 (H1 - lexical commitment can precede concept resolution): Tests that for these errors the committed first token overtakes early and before the concept is resolved. Data: the premature-lexicalization vs. correct-answer cases from Experiments 3-4. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; tuned-lens locates the layer where the eventual first token overtakes competitors and where the concept probe first recovers the correct entity. Systems compared: concept-correct layer vs. lexical-commitment layer, and committed-token early prior for error vs. correct cases. Decisive metric: fraction of premature-lexicalization errors with concept-correct-layer <= lexical-commitment-layer AND an anomalously early/high first-token prior (first); supporting: distribution of the layer gap. Convincing: >=60% of these errors satisfy both conditions vs a correct-answer base rate <=30%. Undecidable band: 40-60% means the timing signature is inconsistent - report as partial. Negative: <40%, near the correct-case base rate, means premature commitment is not the signature, falsifying H1's timing prediction.

Experiment 6 (H3 - re-weighting lexical commitment recovers the entity more selectively than editing): Tests suppression / concept-conditioned re-ranking against weight editing. Data: held-out premature-lexicalization failures, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME/MEMIT comparators; (a) suppress the committed distractor first-token direction at commitment layers, (b) re-score the first token by projecting the concept representation to constrain candidates; random-direction control; alpha swept; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: suppression / re-ranking vs. ROME vs. MEMIT vs. random. Decisive metric: recovered-per-unit-collateral = recovery / accuracy drop on 200 unrelated facts (first); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% collateral, beating ROME/MEMIT on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage is parity - report as comparable. Negative: recovery <20% or no advantage falsifies the selectivity half of H3.

Experiment 7 (H3 generality - one recipe transfers across relations and models): Tests transfer and architecture-generality. Data: train the suppression/re-ranking identification on one relation subset, apply to held-out relations; reuse the Experiment 1 pool per model. Model: single recipe on Llama-3-8B; repeat Experiments 1, 3, 4, 6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds. Systems compared: cross-relation transfer vs. within-relation oracle; three models per decisive metric. Decisive metric: cross-relation recovery rate and cross-model sign-consistency of the Experiment 3 concentration and Experiment 6 advantage (first); supporting: per-model onset gaps. Convincing: cross-relation recovery >=25% and all three models show the concentration and a recovery advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: transfer 10-25% or the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: <10% transfer or majority model reversal means the mechanism is fact/model-specific.

Experiment 8 (H2 - the failure is driven by first-token statistics): Tests that premature-lexicalization rate rises with adverse first-token statistics. Data: per-fact premature-lexicalization outcomes over the 9,000 facts. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; regress error rate on correct-answer first-token frequency, first-token overlap with high-frequency distractors, and answer token length. Systems compared: first-token-statistics regressors vs. an entity-frequency-only baseline. Decisive metric: partial R^2 of the first-token features beyond entity frequency (first); supporting: sign and magnitude of each coefficient. Convincing: first-token features add partial R^2 >=0.10 with the predicted signs (rare correct first token, common shared distractor token, longer answers all raise the rate). Undecidable band: partial R^2 0.03-0.10 is a weak trend - report as suggestive. Negative: partial R^2 <0.03 means first-token statistics do not drive the failure, falsifying the core mechanistic claim of H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Defining a truly token-agnostic 'concept' probe is hard; alias-based invariance is imperfect and may leak surface information. We use held-out aliases and paraphrastic descriptions and report coverage; the causal patching test (Exp 4) is the decisive evidence rather than probe onset alone.

Premature-lexicalization errors may be rare relative to genuine wrong-concept errors, yielding a small effect; the frequency/similarity-matched baseline is essential and a modest significant effect remains informative.

Concept and lexical stages may be entangled (not cleanly two-stage), weakening the strong dissociation claim; graded results would still be scientifically informative and we report continuous measures.

Suppressing a first-token direction could degrade fluency or introduce new errors when the direction overlaps useful features; strict specificity and perplexity controls are included and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
Analysis focuses on entities where first-token distinctions are meaningful; single-token answers and heavily subword-fragmented names complicate readout, and we report coverage restrictions.
A single transferable intervention recipe may not exist if the failure is fact-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.
